extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and policy-makers interested in peer review and scholarly publishing reform
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and comparing peer review models, practices, and interventions (e.g., anonymity regimes, timing, openness, reviewer crediting) to determine effects on quality, transparency, bias, efficiency, and incentives in scholarly publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of peer review (single blind, double blind, open)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal forms of journal peer review have evolved: single blind (reviewers anonymous, authors known), double blind (both authors and reviewers anonymous), and open (identities or reports are disclosed in some way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single blind is most widely used because it is less onerous and less expensive; double blind requires considerable effort to remove traces of author identity; open peer review introduces substantial additional complexity. See Table 1 for mapping of author/reviewer identity visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-peer review commenting (preprints/public commenting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal commenting and discussion on a publicly available pre-publication manuscript draft (i.e., preprints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Rapid, transparent, public, relatively low cost (free for authors), open commenting. Cons/Risks: Variable uptake, fear of scooping, fear of journal rejection, fear of premature communication. Examples: bioRxiv, SocArXiv, PeerJ pre-prints, Figshare, Zenodo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication formal peer review (editorially-invited evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal and editorially-invited evaluation of research by selected experts prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Editorial moderation provides at least some consistent form of quality control for all published work. Cons/Risks: Non-transparent, impossible to evaluate externally, biased, secretive, exclusive, unclear who 'owns' reviews. Examples: Nature, Science, NEJM, The Lancet, Cell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication formal peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal and optionally-invited evaluation of research by selected experts after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Rapid publication of research, public, transparent, can be editorially-moderated. Cons/Risks: Filtering of 'bad research' occurs after publication, relatively low uptake. Examples: F1000Research, ScienceOpen, RIO, The Winnower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication commenting (informal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal discussion of published research, independent of any formal peer review that may have occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Can be performed on third-party platforms, anyone can contribute, public. Cons/Risks: Comments can be rude or of low quality, comments across multiple platforms lack interoperability, low visibility, low uptake. Examples: PubMed Commons, PeerJ, PLOS ONE, ScienceOpen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees, and often editors, participate interactively to reach a consensus decision and a single set of revisions and comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Iterative, editors sign reports, can be integrated with formal process, deters low quality submissions. Cons/Risks: Can be additionally time-consuming, discussion quality variable, peer pressure and influence can tilt the balance. Examples: eLife, Frontiers, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portable peer review (transferable referee reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can take referee reports to multiple consecutive venues, often administered by a third-party service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Reduces redundancy or duplication, saves time. Cons/Risks: Low uptake by authors, low acceptance by journals, high cost. Examples: BioMed Central journals, NPRC, Rubriq, Peerage of Science, MECA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation services (post-publication recommendation/evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication evaluation and recommendation of significant articles often via a peer-nominated consortium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Crowd-sourced literature discovery, time saving, 'prestige' factor. Cons/Risks: Paid services (subscription only), time consuming on recommender side, exclusive. Examples: F1000Prime, CiteULike, ScienceOpen.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-coupled post-publication annotation services
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments or highlights added directly to highlighted sections of the work; notes can be private or public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Rapid, crowd-sourced and collaborative, cross-publisher, low threshold for entry. Cons/Risks: Non-interoperable, multiple venues, effort duplication, relatively unused, genuine critiques reserved. Examples: PubPeer, Hypothesis, PaperHive, PeerLibrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPR primary criteria (definition of Open Peer Review used in article)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this article, OPR is regarded as a process fulfilling any of the following: (1) Referee names are identified to the authors and the readership; (2) Referee reports are made publicly available under an open license; (3) Peer review is not restricted to invited referees only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPR is heterogeneous in meaning and scope; these three criteria are used here as primary indicators of 'open' practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPR seven open traits
rubrics_metrics.description: A distilled definition comprising seven different open traits: participation, identity, reports, interaction, platforms, pre-review manuscripts, and final-version commenting (Ross-Hellauer, 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these traits to characterize how 'open' a peer review implementation is across multiple dimensions rather than relying on a single label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blind peer review (anonymity approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are not revealed to the authors, but referees are aware of author identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Allows reviewers to view full context of an author’s other work, detection of conflicts of interest, more efficient. Cons/Risks: Prone to bias, authors not protected, exclusive, non-verifiable, referees can often be identified anyway. Examples: Most biomedical and physics journals, PLOS ONE, Science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind peer review (anonymity approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and the referees are reciprocally anonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Increased author diversity in published literature, protects authors and reviewers from bias, more objective. Cons/Risks: Still prone to abuse and bias, secretive, exclusive, non-verifiable, referees can often be identified anyway, time consuming. Examples: Nature, most social sciences journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple-blind peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and their affiliations are reciprocally anonymous to handling editors and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Eliminates geographical, institutional, personal and gender biases, work evaluated based on merit. Cons/Risks: Incompatible with pre-prints, low uptake, non-verifiable. Example: Science Matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private open peer review (referees revealed to authors pre-publication if they agree)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee names are revealed to the authors pre-publication, if the referees agree, either through an opt-in or opt-out mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Protects referees, no fear of reprisal for critical reviews. Cons/Risks: Increases decline-to-review rates, non-verifiable. Examples: PLOS Medicine, Learned Publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unattributed (anonymous-but-public) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: If referees agree, their reports are made public but anonymous when the work is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Reports publicized for context and re-use. Cons/Risks: Prone to abuse and bias, secretive, exclusive, non-verifiable. Example: EMBO Journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: As single blind peer review, except that the referees are given the option to make their review and their name public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Increased transparency. Cons/Risks: Gives an unclear picture of the review process if not all reviews are made public. Examples: PeerJ, Nature Communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication open peer review (publishing review history if article accepted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are identified to authors pre-publication, and if the article is published, the full peer review history together with the names of the associated referees is made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Transparency, increased integrity of reviews. Cons/Risks: Fear referees may decline to review or be unwilling to be too critical or positive. Examples: some BMC-series journals, The BMJ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee reports and the names of the referees are always made public regardless of the outcome of their review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Fast publication, transparent process. Cons/Risks: Fear referees may decline to review or be unwilling to be too critical or positive. Examples: F1000Research, ScienceOpen, PubPub.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review by endorsement (PRE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-arranged and invited, with referees providing a 'stamp of approval' on publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros/Benefits: Transparent, cost-effective, rapid, accountable. Cons/Risks: Low uptake, prone to selection bias, not viewed as credible. Examples: RIO Journal, ScienceOpen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing referee reports (report disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making referee reports public to provide increased context and transparency about the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: Provides insights otherwise hidden, enables accountability, educational benefits (training, journal clubs), allows analysis of how authors respond to reviews, and may encourage civility. Risks/observations: Little or no impact on overall process in some studies; can increase decline rates and time to write reviews though not necessarily affecting quality; unclear readership/uptake; unresolved issues about ownership and reuse rights of reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit, recognition, and incentives for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms to recognize and reward peer reviewers (traditional acknowledgements, listing best reviewers, platforms like Publons, integration with ORCID, remuneration in rare cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional methods: thank-you notes, yearly lists, naming best reviewers. Increasing demand: surveys show reviewers value feedback/acknowledgment above payment; formal recognition could motivate participation. Platforms: Publons (review crediting and ranking), ORCID integration, F1000Research/ScienceOpen linking reviews to DOIs. Caveat: commercial publishers have incentives to maintain free reviewer labor; uptake depends on tenure/promotion committees adopting review activity as assessment criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies to reduce reviewer fatigue and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Options include increasing the total pool of potential referees, increasing acceptance rates to avoid review duplication, decreasing the number of referees per paper, and decreasing the time spent on peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-offs: Decreasing number of referees or time spent can reduce review quality. Widening reviewer pool and standardizing peer review activity metadata (e.g., CASRAI recommendations, ORCID linkage) can help. Note empirical evidence that a small minority of researchers perform the majority of reviews and that incentives/crediting could help broaden participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transparency as an indicator of peer review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency (e.g., publishing peer review histories) can be used as an indicator for peer review quality and may predict journal quality in new journals where the peer review model is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Journals with higher transparency ratings were less likely to accept flawed papers and showed higher impact (Google Scholar h5-index). Publishing reports may lengthen comments and improve constructive dialogue, but effects vary by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review should itself be peer reviewed (empirical reproducibility of selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to reproduce how peer review selects what is worthy of publication show the process is generally adequate for detecting reliable research but often fails to recognize the research that has the greatest impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Peer review processes should be subject to systematic study/reproducibility to assess their effectiveness, biases, and failure modes (e.g., gate-keeping errors, failure to detect fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating bias and gatekeeping (anonymity, triple-blind, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity regimes aim to reduce ad hominem evaluations and biases (e.g., gender, institution, geography), while open models trade anonymity for transparency and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blind can increase acceptance rates for under-represented groups but is hard to fully implement; triple-blind attempts to further eliminate biases but has low uptake and incompatibility with preprints. Anonymity can protect reviewers but may enable aggressive or biased behavior; openness can deter conflicts of interest but may reduce willingness to review or critical candor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing linguistic inequality for non-native English speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review conducted by and for non-native English speaking authors can lead to linguistic inequality and language-oriented research segregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider policy/practice adjustments to avoid disadvantaging non-native speakers as research becomes globally competitive; recognize this as a systemic criterion when evaluating peer review fairness.
